meaning.evidence: Every instruction survives in order, including the play-dead split: "keep your pack on and PLAY DEAD", "DO NOT PLAY DEAD", "do NOT play dead—fight back!". "not something to eat" renders 'not a prey animal' accurately.

sense.evidence: Most terms fit: "Getting your tucker", "Clear out of the area", "a sniff". "most bears don't want to have a go at you" works (have a go at = attack), though 'have a go at' often means to criticise.

authenticity.evidence: Plain, natural Australian English: "Pick up small kids straight away", "Help the bear work out that you're a human", "Every situation's different". Nothing staged.

register.evidence: A light touch, mostly in plain casual phrasing rather than slang: "tucker" once, "have a go at you", "Clear out". Right weight for level 2, perhaps a shade light.

tone.evidence: Stays a calm, serious safety notice: "Do NOT run or make any sudden movements.", "Above all, keep your distance from bears!"

flow.evidence: Reads cleanly; the original's repeated line is kept as is ("Don't make any loud noises or screams—the bear might think it's the sound of a prey animal." twice), which is the source's own repetition.

variety.evidence: Little slang to vary; "tucker" sits beside "your food" in the next lines ("get at your food. Getting your tucker"), which is mixed rather than leaned on.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the park-service advice, structure and capitalised warnings intact: "Brown/Grizzly Bears: If you're attacked by a brown/grizzly bear, keep your pack on and PLAY DEAD."

problems.quote: most bears don't want to have a go at you
problems.original: most bears do not want to attack you
problems.why: 'Have a go at' commonly means to criticise or pick on; in a safety notice a plain 'attack' is clearer.

problems.quote: Do NOT let the bear get at your food. Getting your tucker
problems.original: Do NOT allow the bear access to your food. Getting your food
problems.why: Switches from 'food' to 'tucker' mid-thought; reads as a token swap.

A.summary: A clear, accurate and natural casual rendering of the safety advice with a light Aussie touch; tone intact.

meaning.evidence: All instructions kept: "leave your pack on and PLAY DEAD", "DO NOT PLAY DEAD", "Always leave the bear a way out." "groups put bears off as well" softens 'intimidating' a little but keeps the point.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "Pick up littlies straight away", "Do NOT let the bear get at your tucker", "Getting a feed off you". "make things worse for the next lot of people" fits 'worse for others'. "having your head in the right place beforehand" fits 'mentally prepared'.

authenticity.evidence: Natural: "Mind you, check the advice for each park you visit", "If the bear's staying put", "Getting a feed off you". Sounds like an Australian ranger talking.

register.evidence: Light, even slang for level 2: "littlies", "tucker", "a feed", "the next lot", "Mind you". No swearing.

tone.evidence: Serious and calm throughout: "Do NOT run, but if the bear follows, stop and hold your ground.", "fight back!"

flow.evidence: Smooth; colons replace dashes cleanly ("Don't make any loud noises or screams: the bear may think"). "having your head in the right place beforehand can help you react the best way you can" is slightly long.

variety.evidence: "tucker" twice in consecutive lines ("get at your tucker", "getting into your tucker"); otherwise varied.

essence.evidence: The same document, retold: headings, caps warnings and the grizzly/black-bear contrast all present.

problems.quote: stop a bear getting into your tucker
problems.original: prevent a bear from accessing your food
problems.why: 'tucker' in back-to-back paragraphs; a little leaned on.

B.summary: A well-judged level-2 rendering: accurate, natural, calm and lightly Aussie.

meaning.evidence: All instructions kept: "leave your pack on and PLAY DEAD", "DO NOT PLAY DEAD", "do NOT play dead—fight back!". "Bushwalk and get about in groups" localises 'Hike and travel'. "a group's big enough to put a bear off" keeps 'intimidating'.

sense.evidence: Mostly exact: "Once a bear's clocked you", "Pick up any littlies straight away", "go up heaps". "if she reckons you're a danger to her cubs" strains slightly: 'reckons' gives a bear an opinion where the original says 'perceives'.

authenticity.evidence: Natural local voice: "Bushwalk and get about in groups", "wait till the bear moves off", "anything you can lay your hands on". Unforced.

register.evidence: Light-to-moderate: "clocked", "littlies", "tucker", "heaps", "reckons", "Bushwalk". Fits level 2, perhaps a hair over.

tone.evidence: Stays a sober safety notice: "Do NOT run or make any sudden movements.", "Above all, keep your distance from bears!"

flow.evidence: Reads well; one long joined sentence: "A group's usually noisier and smellier than one person on their own, so bears tend to pick up on a group from further off, and with all of you together, a group's big enough to put a bear off, too."

variety.evidence: Varied: "clocked", "littlies", "tucker", "Bushwalk", "get about", "heaps", "till". "tucker" twice in neighbouring paragraphs.

essence.evidence: Plainly the same park advice, every section and caps warning retained.

problems.original: if she perceives you as a danger to her cubs
problems.why: 'Reckons' (thinks, judges) sits oddly on a bear's instinctive perception.

problems.quote: a group's big enough to put a bear off, too

C.summary: A natural, well-localised retelling (Bushwalk, clocked) that keeps every instruction and the serious tone; one strained 'reckons'.

meaning.evidence: Every instruction kept, since the text is the original: "leave your pack on and PLAY DEAD", "DO NOT PLAY DEAD".

sense.evidence: The swaps fit: "Pick up littlies immediately", "Getting your tucker", "accessing your tucker".

authenticity.evidence: The rest is untouched US agency prose: "additional strategies can help prevent the situation from escalating", "Moving sideways is also non-threatening to bears". Slang words are dropped into formal sentences: "prevent a bear from accessing your tucker".

register.evidence: Largely untranslated: only "littlies", "tucker" and spelling ("behaviour", "recognise") change. Well under a level-2 brief.

tone.evidence: The original's serious tone survives because the text does: "Do NOT run or make any sudden movements."

flow.evidence: Reads like the original, including its slip "based local bear behaviour"; the slang inside formal clauses jars: "prevent a bear from accessing your tucker".

variety.evidence: Two slang words, "tucker" used twice ("Getting your tucker", "accessing your tucker").

D.summary: Essentially the original with 'littlies', 'tucker' and Australian spelling; accurate but barely retold.

meaning.evidence: Every instruction kept, with elaborations that hang off the original: "so you're not outrunning it", "so up a tree is no escape", "That's the opposite of the grizzly, so get it straight." The asides "(no offence to your mates)" and "Don't panic if it does" are colour.

sense.evidence: Terms fit well: "just having a stickybeak, not squaring up to you" for curious not threatening, "don't want a bar of attacking you", "peeling off at the last second", "it won't rattle the bear", "go through the roof".

authenticity.evidence: A real Australian voice: "don't want a bar of", "stickybeak", "scores a feed off you", "their patch", "If you cop an attack from a black bear". Idiom used the way locals use it.

register.evidence: Heavier than level 2: a chatty retelling with many idioms and added asides ("(no offence to your mates)", "So a bear's clocked you", "These are general tips, mind.", "Hike and travel in a mob"). Closer to a level 3-4.

tone.evidence: Mostly serious, but jokey asides lighten a life-safety notice: "(no offence to your mates)", "so get it straight". The core warnings stay firm: "Do NOT run."

flow.evidence: Reads aloud easily; it even smooths the original's duplicated line with "And again, because it matters:". A slightly cluttered opening: "Every park's got its own advice, so check it for each park you visit: the local bears don't all carry on the same way, so the advice changes from park to park."

variety.evidence: Wide spread with no tics: "clocked", "twigs", "whiff", "stickybeak", "a bar of", "peeling off", "mob", "scores a feed", "patch", "cop".

essence.evidence: Still the park-service guidance with its sections and caps warnings, retold as advice from a mate.

problems.why: An added joke that lightens a safety notice and pushes past a level-2 brief.

problems.why: Useful emphasis, but a bossy added line heavier than the brief.

problems.original: recommendations do vary from park to park based local bear behavior
problems.why: The opening paragraph says the same thing twice ('check it for each park ... changes from park to park').

E.summary: The most idiomatic and lively version, accurate throughout, but well heavier and chattier than a level-2 safety notice calls for.
